entries.title: Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1
entries.summary: <p>Back when the idea of an elected school board was still being debated, opponents voiced fears that the powerful Chicago Teachers Union would simply try to buy the elections.</p><p>Yet as Chicago stands on a historic precipice of electing all<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u> 20 members and a citywide president</u></a> on Nov. 3 that’s not how it’s playing out.</p><p>Cash is flooding the election but the bulk<b> </b>so far has come from wealthy, often suburban donors, whose political groups have outraised the CTU five to 1 and outspent the teachers union nearly three to 1, according to an analysis of the most recent campaign finance filings between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div style="min-height:311px" id="datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/full.png" alt="A bar chart with four blue bars of different lengths. The headline reads, “Spending by PACs and super PACs”. The description below reads, “Money that has gone to support or oppose CPS School Board candidates between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026”. The bars are sorted from longest to shortest, and each one’s length indicates a dollar amount. At the top, the first bar is nearly double the length of the next. That top bar is labeled “Common Ground Collective” and lists an amount of $3.81 million. Below it is a bar for “Illinois Network of Charter Schools” and an amount of $2.08 million. Next, in a bar that is roughly halved yet again in length from the one before, is “Chicago Teachers Union” with $0.92 million. And below that, slightly shorter, is “Service Employees International Union” with $0.69 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Charter school backers and a few prominent billionaires aligned in a shared antipathy for the teachers union have aimed their millions attacking the Chicago Teacher Union’s choice for board president rather than at bolstering any particular candidate, the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis shows.</p><p>More than a quarter<b> </b>of the $8.1 million total<b> </b>spent on all races so far by these political action committees and the independent expenditure committees, known as super PACs, has targeted a single candidate: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a>.</p><p>The spending to oppose Dominguez is more than four times the amount spent on the top supported candidate, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a>, one of the other two candidates for school board president.</p><p>Biggs, a former CPS principal, has attracted wide-ranging contributions from labor unions other than the CTU, former CPS leaders and investment bankers and CEOs — such as Michael Sacks of GCM Grosvenor and Paul Finnegan of Madison Dearborn Partners.</p><p>Both Biggs and Dominguez have directly raised about $1 million. Defense attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, who lent himself $500,000, trails in fundraising with no support from special interest groups, unions or PACs — <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/4-takeaways-from-cps-school-board-president-forum" target="_blank" ><u>something he touts</u></a>.</p><p>Arnie Rivera, CPS former chief operating officer<b> </b>who heads a new advocacy group called the Chicago Education Alliance, says the billionaire-funded political groups see the school board races as an opportunity to take down the CTU ahead of the mayoral race in February. Mayor Brandon Johnson remains closely allied with the union, which helped catapult their former organizer to office. Some of the $12.7 million raised by three education-focused political action committees currently spending big will almost certainly be deployed in the mayor’s race.</p><p>“It just becomes a proxy battle on the political side,” Rivera says. “CTU is a huge political group here in the city, and I think you have people who are trying to push back on it. I think that is what it comes down to.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-980000" name="html-embed-module-980000"></a><div style="min-height:611px" id="datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/full.png" alt="A chart with five rectangles, all stacked vertically in one column together. A headline reads, “CTU-endorsed candidate for board president is the main target of PAC spending”. The description below it says, “Powerful outside groups have spent about $8.1 million on the school board election so far. More than a quarter has gone to oppose Hilario Dominguez, the Chicago Teachers Union’s pick for president.” The chart’s top two rectangles are different shades of orange, and the bottom three are different shades of gray; a thick black line separates the orange section from the gray section. Above the chart is a label: “Spending by political action committees and Super PACs, in millions of dollars”. The orange rectangles represent spending in opposition of particular candidates, and together they take up about two-fifths of the chart’s overall height. The gray rectangles represent spending in support of particular candidates, and together they take up the other three-fifths or so of the chart’s overall height. The topmost portion of the chart is a brightly colored orange rectangle showing $2.30 million spent opposing Hilario Dominguez; below that is a light orange rectangle showing $0.98 million spent opposing candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez. In the gray section, looking from the other end, there is a small, dark gray rectangle showing $0.58 million spent supporting Dominguez, followed by a similarly sized and lighter gray rectangle showing $0.53 million spent supporting Jessica Biggs. Above those (so in the middle between them and the orange opposition spending) is a large, light gray rectangle showing $3.79 million spent supporting candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez or Biggs." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The latest campaign finance reports from the Illinois State Board of Elections, which were due by midnight Thursday, show an escalation of cash and spending in the last three months, both directly by the campaigns, as well as by outside groups on their behalf.</p><p>The 43 total candidates vying for board seats have directly raised another $4.1 million since the end of June, adding up to $5.9 million in contributions since October 2025. Since August, four candidates have withdrawn. There are also four write-in candidates.</p><p>Candidates just for the board president position account for $3.5 million,<b> </b>including contributions for two who recently dropped out.</p><p>Twenty local district races, 15 of which are contested, split the remaining $2.4 million. Eleven races have accumulated more than $100,000, with one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/1b/" target="_blank" ><u>competitive Northwest Side race in District 1b</u></a> pulling in $292,062 in contributions.</p><p>None of the five district candidates running unopposed are aligned with the CTU. Current school board members <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/4b/" target="_blank" ><u>Ellen Rosenfeld</u></a> have raised $100,000 each.</p><p>“I'm open to taking money from anybody,” Smith says, noting that he also has gotten donations from SEIU, the union that represents support staff in CPS. “But I'll tell you one thing that's interesting: they never asked me to vote a certain way. They never have given a policy and said, ‘Push that through.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div><p></p><h4><b>Big money coming from a new outside group</b></h4><p>The real money in these races is being raised and spent outside the campaigns via a series of political action committees and super PACs. The latter face no limits on how much they can raise or spend, as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates.</p><p>In addition to wealthy charter school supporters who typically amass and spend<b> </b>when school issues are at stake, billionaire Sacks has dropped millions attacking the Chicago Teachers Union candidates via his newly formed Common Ground Collective super PAC.</p><p>That group has spent the most so far, $3.7 million on digital ads and production, about half of it attacking Dominguez, a teacher-turned-CTU deputy political director.</p><p>The group has yet to endorse or fund ads in support of anyone for board president, though Sacks himself gave $400,000 to Biggs earlier this month.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>A key behind-the-scenes ally</u></a> to former Mayor Rahm Emanuel — who long fought with the CTU — Sacks has given the most money to any of the groups funding the school board elections, $5.5 million as of October 15.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-300000" name="image-300000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Michael Sacks, on the left, with business and civic leader John Rogers, has poured millions into the Chicago School Board race to try to undercut Chicago Teachers Union candidates. He has donated $5.5 million to groups involved with the school board election.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Close on his heels with $3.8 million is Jim Frank, a retired executive from Winnetka<b>, </b>and regular major donor to the Illinois Network of Charter Schools’ political spending groups.</p><p>The INCS Action super PAC has spent $450,000 on a digital ad opposing Dominguez, but only $1,000 supporting one candidate for president who has since dropped out.<b> </b>INCS’ political arms have not made any endorsement for president.</p><p>Outspent by the CTU in 2024, the INCS Action groups have also spent an additional $1.7 million supporting 19 candidates currently in board races,<b> </b>including to candidates who face no opponent.</p><p>Representatives from Common Ground Collective and INCS declined interview requests.</p><p>Dominguez says money isn’t everything.</p><p>“What I'll say is this — that we didn't go from mayoral control to go to billionaire control, right?” Dominguez says. “At no point in this race did we think we were going to be beating billionaires in spending money. One thing that we've seen and we're seeing across the entire country is that organized people beats organized money any day of the week.”</p><h4>Spending big to make a splash </h4><p>The third group aligned in this election against the teachers union is The Urban Center, though its donations and spending are dwarfed by INCS and the Common Ground Collective.</p><p>Juan Rangel, the executive director of the center, which promotes school choice across public and private schools, said if you want to make an impact, you need to spend big money. That requires first educating people that a school board race is happening and explaining what’s at stake.</p><p>“I would hope that people would understand that these school board elections are the most important races on the November ballot, and they will have implications and ramifications to the February mayoral election," Rangel says.</p><p>What’s different about Chicago is that the wealthy billionaires are local, rather than outsiders pushing a conservative agenda, says Jeffrey R. Henig, a professor emeritus at Columbia University's Teachers College, who co-wrote the book, “Outside Money in School Board Elections: The Nationalization of Education Politics.”</p><p>“I'm struck by … the lack of sharp ideological cleavages and the relative absence of the culture war politics that you see in a lot of suburban districts,” he says. For example, no one is pushing book bans.</p><p>He also points out differences between candidates are more subtle than in ones where big national social issues are at play, so “instead of eliminating charter schools in Chicago, it's about how and under what extreme circumstances we might close some schools.”</p><p>Teacher unions usually enjoy a built-in advantage, regardless of money, Henig says. That’s because teachers and parents with a vested interest in what happens in schools are the most likely to show up and actually vote in school board elections.</p><h3>Is CTU spending coming?</h3><p>The CTU ended up outspending everyone else two years ago — $4.3 million via two political action committees, with about half dropping in the last month.</p><p>It’s been slower so far this time in unrolling campaign ads.</p><p>The CTU has disclosed raising about $2.5 million and spent about $2.2 million through its political organization as well as Our Schools PAC, which it funds.</p><p>“What is unusual in spending in a race is spending a tremendous amount of money not for somebody for president but against somebody,” says CTU Pavlyn Jankov, the union’s research director.</p><p>“We’re never going to compete with the billionaires in this race, and our members support our candidates, so we're going to be continuing to put our money into this race because it reflects the values of 30,000 members.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-580000" name="html-embed-module-580000"></a><div style="min-height:353px" id="datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/full.png" alt="A column chart with four columns, each representing a dollar amount spent in a given month. The headline reads, “How the Chicago Teachers Union rolled out its political spending in 2024”. The description below reads, “Spending by CTU’s political action committee and related PACs on school board races in first school board election, by month”. Below that, the chart shows a column (i.e., a bar stretching vertically) for each month from August through November 2024. The first two (August and September) are much shorter than the remaining two (October and November). August 2024 has an amount of about $164,100. September has an amount of about $301,700. October has an amount (again, much larger than the preceding one) of $1.7 million. November has the slightly smaller amount of $1.6 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>More contributions and spending still could come. Like most labor unions, its coffers get replenished through member dues. CTU leaders tried in vain last spring to get members to increase dues, which could have gone toward political spending.</p><p>Robert Bruno, director of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign’ labor education department and author of a book about the 2012 CTU strike, says the union’s resources have been stretched lately, by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/17/chicago-teachers-union-illinois-policy-institute-defamation-lawsuit-stacy-davis-gates" target="_blank" ><u>lawsuits</u></a> as well as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/ctu-to-cooperate-with-congressional-inquiry-over-financial-audits-chicago-teachers-union" target="_blank" ><u>federal probes</u> — and other elections.</a></p><p>“I can't help but also acknowledge that in addition to this first-ever school board race, there's also the mayoral race, and there's a lot of competition. And that competition involves candidates who have raised a fair amount of money, can raise a lot of money, and obviously, if Mayor Johnson's going to get reelected, he's going to need a very, very highly engaged and supportive Chicago Teachers Union.”</p><p>Plus, he notes, Biggs is no enemy to labor, squarely backed by SEIU.</p><h4>The CTU-SEIU union split</h4><p>Another factor in this election is that the SEIU, the union that represents support staff, has split from its once-close ally, the CTU, after accusing the teachers union of trying to raid some of their members. And they’ve split on most of their candidate endorsements, parting ways on 10 endorsements, including board president. They only overlap on five endorsements</p><p>But Anthony Driver, the chair of a new SEIU-funded PAC Brighter Futures, warned against lumping his union with the other political groups that are anti-CTU.</p><p>“We are not a corporate PAC,” he says. “If anything we are a PAC that operates similarly to the CTU.”</p><p>“We represent low wage workers who are largely erased,” he says, “and it becomes a question of who gets to be heard.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-910000" That’s the same for individual school board candidates like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/carlos-a-rivas-jr/" target="_blank" ><u>Carlos Rivas Jr.</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a>. “They have stood with us,” Driver says.</p><p>He also pointed out that union PACs have a finite amount of money and so hold their spending until the last few weeks of an election, whereas PACs supported by corporate backers have more resources so can maintain high spending throughout.</p><p>Driver also notes that SEIU is only spending to support candidates, not oppose them.</p><p>Henig said it is not unusual for unions supporting teachers and school district support staff to support different candidates. After all, when it comes to budget cuts, they do not have the same interests.</p><p>Chicago was the outlier, Driver says, which is ”what made us able to build power.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7f0000" name="module-7f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election. entries.title: 4 Chicago area congressional offices receive suspicious letters amid wave of preelection threats
entries.summary: <p>The offices of four Democratic state representatives each received suspicious letters Friday. </p><p>Reps. Brad Schneider, Mike Quigley, Robin Kelly and Jan Schakowsky reported being sent the letters in a broader wave of threatening packages mailed to congressional and state election offices nationwide ahead of Election Day in November. </p><p>The reports come as <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/15/nx-s1-6003857/suspicious-mailings-election-congressional-offices" target="_blank" >similar suspicious mail</a> has been sent to election officials and representatives in several states, including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma, NPR reported.</p><p>Schneider’s office, which is located in Linconshire, contacted Lincolnshire and U.S. Capitol police after receiving the suspicious letter. It was ultimately deemed to not contain harmful substances by law enforcement.</p><p>Quigley’s office at 1925 N. Clybourn Ave. was also evacuated as a precaution Friday when a suspicious letter arrived there. Schakowsky's Skokie office didn't open the letter after warnings from the House sergeant-at-arms.</p><p>Schneider said the FBI is looking into the rash of threatening letters. The bureau didn’t immediately respond to a request for details on the investigation.</p><p>"It is imperative that [the FBI] follow all leads to apprehend and prosecute those responsible,” Schneider said in a statement. "Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken."</p><p>Kelly said her team immediately contacted the U.S. Capitol Police, which she said is also investigating the incident. The police force didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Elections <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" target="_blank" ><u>evacuated its offices</u></a> Thursday when it received a suspicious letter, which was taken as part of the investigation by the FBI. A similar<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" target="_blank" ><u> suspicious envelope</u></a> containing baking powder was delivered to Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ downtown office at 118 N. Clark St. also on Thursday.</p><p>“Political violence has no place in a democracy, and efforts to scare or intimidate the public in the lead-up to an election must be resoundingly condemned,” Quigley said in a statement. “I hope that the perpetrator is swiftly brought to justice.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" >Feds investigating ‘suspicious’ letter sent to Chicago election office</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" >Pappas office receives envelope with ‘suspicious’ substance, turns out to be baking powder</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Insufficient evidence that Chicago School Board candidate engaged in sexual misconduct, watchdog report finds
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools’ watchdog determined there was insufficient evidence that Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, engaged in sexual misconduct with a CPS student nearly a decade ago, in part because there were no eyewitnesses to the alleged behavior and her allegations did not point to a “sustained pattern of behavior.”</p><p>The 34-page report, obtained by WBEZ Friday through an open records request, notes that when the inspector general’s office first opened its case in 2021, it did so because CPS was notified that a Pilsen-based nonprofit had investigated Dominguez in 2018 for alleged conduct “that raised grooming concerns.”</p><p>But after interviewing the young woman who raised the allegations, investigators said the two incidents she recalled that made her feel uncomfortable in 2017, when she was 17 years old, were “less indicative of sexual misconduct” and “narrower in scope” than the internal report filed with the nonprofit.</p><p>The inspector general’s office said the woman alleged that Dominguez asked “about her dating preferences on one occasion” and physically picked her up “holding her body against his, and swinging her from side to side on another occasion.” After she complained to staff at The Resurrection Project, the nonprofit where she participated in a summer jobs program, Dominguez “never made her uncomfortable again.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>The reopened investigation</u></a>, coming just weeks before voters head to the polls, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>has roiled the heated race for school board president</u></a>. Dominguez, a former CPS teacher and former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, has denied the allegations and said they were surfaced by Aida Flores, a former political opponent who ran against him for a City Council seat in 2019.</p><p>The inspector general’s office said the upcoming election was not a factor in reopening the investigation, and that the young woman did not seem to have a political motive to first report the alleged behavior to The Resurrection Project in 2017.</p><p>The CPS watchdog reopened its investigation last month after the young woman, who is now 26, called that office and said she hadn’t known about the investigation and wanted a chance to speak with investigators.</p><p>“The political backdrop is relevant but should not distract from the question at the heart of this investigation: whether Dominguez attempted to groom [redacted name] for a sexual purpose or sexually harassed her,” the report states. “Given that those allegations were not otherwise corroborated by the evidence, the OIG did not have to consider the issue of political motivation to determine that the allegations against Dominguez are not substantiated.”</p><p>If the incidents did happen, the inspector general’s office wrote, it was also unclear if they were sexually motivated. The office said it’s possible the behavior the young woman described could have been “part of an ill-advised matchmaking effort or attempt to relate to her as a mentor.”</p><p>And while the alleged conduct, alongside the available evidence, didn’t meet the school district’s threshold for grooming or sexual harassment, the inspector general’s office said the alleged conduct would not be acceptable for a CPS staffer and noted that it would violate CPS’ current standards for boundaries between staff and students.</p><p>But those standards did not yet exist in 2017 and Dominguez was on a break from working at CPS at the time.</p><p>Earlier this week, Rima Kapitan, a lawyer for Dominguez, said the inspector general’s report “fully cleared” Dominguez of any wrongdoing.</p><p>Dominguez <a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>said in a statement on Wednesday</u></a> that he now wants to “re-center his campaign” on education issues.</p><p>In a statement provided to WBEZ through her lawyer, the young woman said the process for investigating her claims had been “deeply flawed.”</p><p>“Like so many victims and survivors undermined by a broken system before me, I know what happened to me, and I am not going to be silenced,” she wrote. “While I am disappointed in the failure of this report to affirmatively verify my experience, it certainly does not exonerate Hilario Dominguez, or ‘clear him in full,’ as he claims.”</p><p>The inspector general’s office attempted to reach the young woman and her parents on 12 occasions in 2022, including leaving several voicemails for her mother and father as well as direct messages to the woman’s social media accounts, according to the report. It adds that the woman’s mother “would have been familiar with the OIG and would have been trained” on sexual misconduct investigation practices within CPS.</p><p>Additionally, investigators reviewed text messages that were “potentially inconsistent” with some of the young woman’s claims. She told the inspector general’s office that Dominguez had reached out to her on two occasions to set up a meeting in 2020 and 2022.</p><p>However, text messages show that it was the young woman, not Dominguez, who reached out for a meeting in 2022, including suggesting they meet alone. The meeting never took place.</p><p>The report adds that the potential inconsistencies could exist because the exchanges took place a long time ago.</p><p>In a statement Friday, Inspector General Philip Wagenknecht stressed that his office is apolitical and that its investigation began long before the school board president race kicked off this year. He said the investigation was in “no way” rushed or “concluded prematurely.”</p><p>“No one outside this office has influence over how OIG investigations are handled, and there were no external efforts to influence this matter,” he wrote.</p><p>The report cited “heavy caseload and limited resources” for the reason that it took five years to close the initial investigation.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>The young woman’s lawyer sent letters Wednesday</u></a> to the inspector general, CPS board members and the district’s superintendent calling for an independent review of how the inspector general’s office investigated this case.</p><p>Sixteen City Council members also called for an independent investigation Thursday, claiming the process was “tainted.”</p><p>“The Mayor’s hand-picked CPS Inspector General rushed a finding to meet the deadline he publicly demanded, sending a devastating message to every girl weighing whether to report abuse,” the members said in a statement.</p><p>A spokesperson for the mayor’s office said that “at no point” did it contact the inspector general’s office during its investigation or “make any attempt” to exert influence.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sarah Karp</i></p><div entries.title: Six months after the Sky traded her away, Angel Reese is in the WNBA Finals
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — The thing that I’ve always found spookiest about former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" ><u>Sky</u></a> star Angel Reese is the way she speaks things into existence.</p><p>She’d put pretty much every accomplishment this year — from making the FIBA World Cup team to being named Defensive Player of the Year to reaching her first WNBA Finals — out into the universe well beforehand.</p><p>She calls it manifesting.</p><p>I remember being caught off guard by her manifesting last season, when she casually dropped in a pregame interview that she was planning on becoming Defensive Player of the Year. I’d always thought of her as a good, instinctive defender, but she, at 23 years old, thought she could dethrone the likes of A’ja Wilson and Napheesa Collier?</p><p>She could and she did. Impressive stuff.</p><p>But what I most enjoyed about covering Reese, in the two years before the Sky traded her to the Dream, was the way she made you think. My questions about her ranged from the little mysteries to the big ones.</p><p>Little: Why could she outjump anybody for a rebound, but when she shot a layup, seemed to dive toward the rim and windshield-wiper the ball up?</p><p>Big: What made her work so ravenously toward her goals? Would she ever view life as something other than a set of stages to be conquered? Would she look back the way she looks forward?</p><p>I asked her about this Friday, on the eve of Game 1 in San Francisco, reminding her that as a rookie, she once told us that she didn’t really ever have time to reflect. Now that she was in a slightly different moment in her life, had that changed? Her answer was basically no.</p><p>“I think my journey speaks for itself,” she said. “A year ago I was walking in [the Victoria's Secret fashion show] for the first time ever. Now a year later I’m on the biggest stage and being able to be in the Finals.</p><p>“I haven’t had time to really reflect yet. Maybe the offseason is time, but I always have something going on in the off season, so it’s really hard.</p><p>“But I think like: I work hard now in my 20s, my early 30s so I can rest and relax and have a family and do all the other fun things when I’m older.”</p><p>Fair enough: she can leave the reflecting to the writers and the old folk while she marches on.</p><p>I still think about Reese’s time in Chicago often. I can picture waking up to the subject heading in my inbox on that fateful Monday in April: “Chicago Sky Trade Angel Reese to the Atlanta Dream, Acquire Draft Picks.”</p><p>I groaned. It was <i>just</i> like the Sky to recognize her potential while others doubted her, trade valuable draft capital to get her, and then fail to make it work long-term.</p><p>I knew Reese’s short tenure was a huge opportunity blown for the franchise, and that her departure would hurt fans. Personally, though, I was ambivalent. I’d miss her booming presence, but I was glad to be done with the mess of haters and rabid defenders around her. With the Sky in such a steep decline, I wasn’t sure any one player could turn things around.</p><p>When I sat down to write, the first thing that came to mind was the story of Jack and the Beanstalk. The protagonist, Jack, is sent by his family to sell their cow, but to their dismay, Jack returns with a bag of magic beans.</p><p><i>The Sky traded forward Angel Reese to the Dream on Monday for a bag of magic beans,</i> I wrote. That may have captured how fans felt in the moment, but it wasn’t totally accurate — in the English fairy tale, the beans actually end up saving Jack’s family. In this story, they won’t. The only immediate return the Sky will get from the Dream this offseason is the No. 12 pick in the 2027 draft. The last time the Sky drafted that late in the first round, they ended up with the not-exactly-franchise-changing services of Hailey Van Lith.</p><p>The best hope for the Sky is that the “beans” grow into a lesson: if you trade up to draft an alpha star like Reese, you need a robust plan to see it through.</p><p>What Reese has taught me is that great players change your understanding of what, exactly, greatness looks like. I thought her layup form might limit her, but I was wrong. She’s now anchoring a Finals team, averaging 18 points and 8 rebounds in the playoffs. She’s doing it with her motor, IQ and, surprisingly, more confidence from three.</p><p>A good reminder to weigh a player’s mindset and desire just as heavily as their form.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Nic Claxton expected to be only Bull not available to start season
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls will be close to 100% healthy when they open the season Wednesday at the Raptors. Only center Nic Claxton, who’s nursing a hamstring injury, won’t be ready. But coach Tiago Splitter said the seven-year veteran is ramping up basketball activities.</p><p>“Every day he does something else and more aggressive,” Splitter said Friday before the Bulls’ preseason finale against the Timberwolves. “But — I’m not going to stop repeating this — this is a very dangerous injury. The chances of redoing it are big. So we’ve got to be careful.”</p><p>Claxton suffered the injury during a training-camp practice early this month. He and center Zach Collins (quad) were seen working out during the morning shootaround at the Advocate Center, Claxton jogging lightly and Collins jumping rope.</p><p>“[Collins is] supposed to be 100%,” Splitter said. “He’s supposed to be in all the practices that we have left. Full contact, everything.”</p><p>Forward Tobe Awaka and guard Isaac Okoro have been out with knee injuries. They joined Collins and Claxton on the sideline Friday.</p><p>Splitter went into the game looking for improvement in several areas.</p><p>“I can give you a list,” he said. “We got to rebound better; we got to take care of the ball; we got to crash more on offense; the ball cannot stick, we got to move the ball side to side. Those are the most important things right now.”</p><p>When Splitter has everyone available, he expects to have a nine-to-10-man rotation most of the time because he wants the Bulls to run.</p><h3>Giddey’s a video star</h3><p>He isn’t yet the “Czar of the Telestrator,” the nickname of former NBA coach and TV analyst Mike Fratello, but Bulls guard Josh Giddey is breaking down game video of himself on his YouTube channel, @OfficialJoshGiddey. He has four videos up and many more to come. Giddey plans to post one every Sunday night.</p><p>“I saw Tom Brady do it on a football game from a quarterback’s perspective,” Giddey said. “I love watching football and the NFL, and I never really understood it on that deep a level. It was really cool to see, and I thought that’s something I could do for basketball.”</p><p>Giddey is a video junkie. Since he’s watching anyway, he figured why not teach fans how he sees the game as a point guard. He takes videos of himself, then sends them to editors who combine his video with the game video and add graphic elements. Giddey’s first video, which posted Sept. 20, was about his game-winning halfcourt shot to beat the Lakers last season.</p><p>“I’ve always loved when top-tier athletes, whatever sport they’re in, have broken it down on a pretty deep level,” said Giddey, who has more than 20,000 subscribers. “It gives fans a better understanding of the game.”</p><h3>Is it Miller’s time?</h3><p>Forward Leonard Miller entered Friday leading the Bulls in preseason scoring with 17.5 points per game. Splitter has been impressed, but he said Miller has more to prove.</p><p>“He’s a mismatch for slower fives,” Splitter said. “We can use him in that position; we can use him at the four position. He’s playing well so far.</p><p>“It’s still only the preseason. Wednesday, when the lights are on, it’s going to be a different game. You’ve got to also think about that.”</p><h3>Time change</h3><p>The Bulls’ game next Friday at the Bucks was moved to 3 p.m. from 7 because it would’ve conflicted with Game 1 of the World Series, which will be in Milwaukee.</p>
